headline: China's economy grows faster than expected

sources.title: China's economy grows 4.5 percent in Q3, beating forecasts (Al Jazeera)
China economy: Growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness (BBC News)
China's third-quarter economic growth quickens to 4.5% as exports surge, beating estimates (CNBC)

chunks.text: New official [[figures]] that {{came out}} on Monday, October 19, 2026, show that China's [[economic growth]] has {{picked up}}. The economy grew 4.5 percent from July to September, compared with the same months in 2025. That was slightly better than most experts expected. Growth had {{slowed down}} to 4.3 percent from April to June, the weakest rate in three years. The government's [[target]] for 2026 is 4.5 to 5 percent.

verbs.why: Exam results come out in the middle of August. A new report on jobs comes out every month. China's new growth figures came out on Monday, October 19, 2026.

verbs.wrong: To be counted in a new way
verbs.why: Sales usually pick up in December. The wind picks up in the afternoon. China's economic growth picked up from July to September.
Growth often slows down as a country gets richer. Home sales slow down in the winter months. China's growth slowed down to 4.3 percent from April to June.

chunks.text: Exports were the main reason for the growth. Chinese factories have {{cashed in on}} a global [[boom]] in artificial intelligence. There is strong [[demand]] for computer chips and other parts for AI [[data centers]]. Production of batteries and [[industrial robots]] grew by more than 29 percent. These strong sales abroad have {{made up for}} weak spending at home. Experts expect China's [[trade surplus]] to beat last year's record of 1.2 trillion dollars.

verbs.correct: To make money from a good chance
verbs.wrong: To lend money to new companies
verbs.why: Hotels cash in on big sports events in their city. Ice cream shops cash in on hot summer days. Chinese factories have cashed in on a global boom in artificial intelligence.

verbs.correct: To balance a weak part with a strong one
verbs.wrong: To hide a weak part from buyers
verbs.why: Good online sales make up for a slow month in the store. A busy summer makes up for a quiet winter at the beach hotel. Strong sales abroad have made up for weak spending at home in China.

chunks.text: Spending at home is much weaker. Many shoppers in China are still {{holding back}}. [[Retail sales]] rose only 1.1 percent in September. An economist said worries about trade have {{put many families off}} spending. Slow [[wage growth]] and high [[youth unemployment]] also hurt. The biggest problem is the [[property market]]. China has struggled for years to {{shake off}} a [[housing slump]]. Property [[investment]] fell by more than 20 percent in the first nine months of 2026.

verbs.correct: To be careful about spending money
verbs.why: Many families hold back when prices are high. Shoppers hold back when they worry about their jobs. Many shoppers in China are still holding back.

verbs.correct: To make someone not want to do something
verbs.wrong: To make prices higher for someone
verbs.why: High prices put many people off buying a new car. Long lines put customers off the new restaurant. Worries about trade have put many Chinese families off spending.

verbs.correct: To get free of a problem
verbs.wrong: To blame others for a problem
verbs.why: Some towns never shake off the loss of a big factory. It takes years to shake off a bad reputation. China has struggled for years to shake off a housing slump.

chunks.text: The government {{stepped up}} its support in late September. It offered lower [[interest rates]] to some businesses and [[subsidies]] for home buyers. Some [[trading partners]], including the U.S. and the European Union, are {{pushing back}} against large amounts of cheap Chinese goods. One economist expects China to {{keep up}} its faster pace for the rest of 2026. A finance professor at Stanford University said a slow, controlled [[slowdown]] is the best the government can hope for.

verbs.why: Police step up patrols on busy weekends. The city steps up its help for poor families in winter. China's government stepped up its support for the economy in late September.

verbs.correct: To show you do not accept something
verbs.wrong: To sell goods at a lower price
verbs.why: Workers push back against longer hours. Parents often push back against new school rules. Some trading partners are pushing back against large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.

verbs.correct: To continue at the same level
verbs.wrong: To change the target for growth
verbs.why: Good runners keep up the same speed for the whole race. Our team needs to keep up this level of work. One economist expects China to keep up its faster pace for the rest of 2026.

mainIdea.s: China's economy grew a bit faster than experts expected from July to September, mostly thanks to strong sales of tech goods abroad. Spending by families and the housing market are still weak.
mainIdea.why: Growth picked up to 4.5 percent because exports were strong. At home, many shoppers are still holding back and the housing slump goes on.

mainIdea.s: Chinese shoppers have started buying far more in stores, and this lifted the economy to its best result in years. Because of that, factories now sell fewer chips and robots to other countries.
mainIdea.why: Close, but it was the other way around. Strong sales abroad made up for weak spending at home, where many shoppers are still holding back.

mainIdea.s: Beijing has announced a plan to build thousands of new factories in poor rural areas of the country. Officials say the project will create millions of jobs for young workers over ten years.
mainIdea.why: The real news is about new growth figures that came out on October 19. Exports helped the economy, while spending at home stayed weak.

tf.s: China's economic growth picked up between July and September.
tf.why: The economy grew 4.5 percent in those months, up from 4.3 percent from April to June.

tf.s: Strong spending at home made up for weak exports.
tf.why: It was the other way around. Strong sales abroad made up for weak spending at home.

tf.s: Chinese factories have cashed in on a global boom in artificial intelligence.
tf.why: There is strong demand for computer chips and other parts for AI data centers.

tf.s: Shoppers in China are now spending freely again.
tf.why: Many shoppers are still holding back, and worries about trade have put many families off spending.

tf.s: Some trading partners are happy to buy more cheap Chinese goods.
tf.why: Some trading partners, including the U.S. and the European Union, are pushing back against large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.

tf.s: China is still struggling to shake off a long housing slump.
tf.why: China has tried for years to shake off the slump, and property investment fell by more than 20 percent.

lines.text: Did you see the new numbers on China's economy?
On Monday. Growth {{picked up}} to 4.5 percent from July to September.
Is that good? I thought it had {{slowed down}}.
It did, earlier in the year. This was a little better than experts expected.
Exports. Chinese factories are {{cashing in on}} the AI boom. Everyone wants their chips.
And people in China? Are they spending more?
Not really. A lot of families are {{holding back}}. They're trying to [[save for a rainy day]].
[[I'm not surprised]]. Housing has been a mess there for years.
Right. The country still can't {{shake off}} that housing slump.
So exports have to {{make up for}} everything else.
Pretty much. But it's risky to put [[all your eggs in one basket]].
True. And other countries are {{pushing back}} against all those cheap goods.
The government {{stepped up}} its help in September, at least.
Will that help families [[on a budget]]?
Maybe. One economist thinks China can {{keep up}} this pace until the end of the year.
Then let's see what the next numbers say.

expressions.def: To keep money for a time in the future when you might need it
ex: My grandmother always told me to save for a rainy day.
We don't spend all our pay. We save for a rainy day.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is what you expected
ex: He was late again? I'm not surprised.

expressions.expr: all your eggs in one basket
expressions.def: Used to say that it is risky to depend on only one thing

expressions.def: Having only a small amount of money to spend
ex: We are on a budget, so we cook at home.
